# Understanding governance proposals

The `glassfrog proposal` commands let an agent or practitioner run the Holacracy
governance write flow: draft a change, circulate it for consent, respond to it,
and withdraw it. This document explains the reasoning behind how that surface is
shaped — why the CLI passes so much through to the server untouched, why it never
pre-checks what it is allowed to do, and where it deliberately stops.

## Why the change set is a verbatim pass-through

A proposal carries a set of governance changes — create a role, add an
accountability, update a policy. You might expect the CLI to offer a typed builder
for each change kind. It does not. Instead `proposal create` takes a JSON array on
`--changes` and forwards it to the server with almost no inspection.

The reason is that the API itself has no per-type schema for a change: a change is
`type` plus open, command-specific keys. There is nothing concrete for the CLI to
validate against. So the client enforces only a minimal floor — the value must be
valid JSON, a non-empty array, and every element must be an object carrying a
non-empty `type` (the one key the schema marks required) — and sends everything
else through byte-for-byte, letting the server be the authority on what each
change means.

The alternative — recognizing each `type` and validating its keys — was
considered and deliberately deferred. Typed change construction is its own problem
(named "Unguided Change Construction" in the project's planning). Building it into
the create command would have coupled a large, evolving concern to a command whose
job is simply to *create*. The tradeoff is that a malformed change is caught by
the server (a `422`) rather than locally, in exchange for a create command that
stays small and never drifts out of sync with the API's change vocabulary.

## Why the CLI never pre-checks transitions or the plan

Two decisions share the same root: the CLI issues the request and lets the server
decide, rather than guessing first.

**Transitions are server-authorized.** A proposal advertises its
`available_transitions` — the actions you may take on it right now. `propose` and
`withdraw` could each read the proposal first to confirm the transition is offered
before sending. They do not. `available_transitions` is server-owned and
time-sensitive; a client-side gate would fork that authority, add a round-trip,
and risk acting on a stale snapshot. So the command sends the transition and
surfaces the server's `422` if it is not allowed.

**The Premium gate is not pre-checked either.** The four write verbs require the
async-proposals feature. The CLI performs no client-side feature check; it always
issues the request and surfaces the server's `403`. Detecting the gate before
sending — and turning a plan-gate `403` into an actionable "not available on your
plan" diagnostic — is a separate capability (Plan-Limit Signal). Until that lands,
the `403` routes through the shared error handling like any other permission
refusal, with no bespoke treatment.

The broader pattern: the CLI is a faithful surface of the API, not a second
rules engine. Re-implementing the server's authorization or plan rules client-side
would mean two sources of truth that can disagree. Letting the server decide keeps
exactly one.

## Why `404` and `422` are real failures, not success

The `propose` and `withdraw` transitions treat a `404` (no such proposal) or a
`422` (transition not allowed) as genuine failures that exit non-zero. This is
worth calling out because a sibling pattern — soft-delete (tension discard) —
treats `404` as *success*, on the logic that a thing that is already gone is in
the state you wanted.

That logic does not apply here. A transition has no idempotent end-state.
Re-proposing an already-circulating proposal is not a harmless no-op — the
proposal no longer offers `propose`, so the `422` is a real refusal the operator
must see. Folding it into success would hide a mistake. The distinction is
deliberate: only operations with a genuine idempotent target absorb a `404`;
transitions never do.

## Why responses are aggregate-only

A proposal carries a `response_summary` — total, no-objection, and bring-to-meeting
counts — but never reveals *who* responded which way, and the CLI does not
reconstruct that from any other field. This is not a limitation the CLI imposes;
the API itself exposes only aggregate counts, an intentional anti-political-pressure
design choice in Holacracy tooling. The CLI honours it by surfacing exactly what
the API returns and manufacturing no attribution it withholds.

The responding person, likewise, is never something you supply — the server
derives it from your token's identity. The CLI operates within that single
identity and must not claim to respond on someone else's behalf.

## Design boundaries

These commands deliberately stop short of several things a "smarter" tool might do:

- **No confirmation prompts.** Even `withdraw`, which deletes existing responses
  server-side, never asks "are you sure?" and offers no `--force`/`--yes` flag.
  The CLI is built for non-interactive, agent-driven use; an interactive guard
  would break that contract. An operator-layer confirmation for destructive writes
  is a separate capability (Write-Safety Guardrail), not these commands' job.
- **No interpretation or facilitation.** The commands do not summarize, advise on,
  or narrate the side effects a write triggers (notifications firing, deadlines
  computed, responses deleted). Those are server-owned consequences, visible only
  through the returned data. The CLI is a faithful API surface, not a Holacracy
  facilitator.
- **No optimistic-concurrency guard on transitions.** `propose`, `respond`, and
  `withdraw` send no `If-Match` precondition. Optimistic concurrency (Guarded
  Writes) applies to field *edits*; a transition or an append-only response create
  has no prior `ETag` to guard against.
- **One capability per command.** `create` only creates, `propose` only advances,
  and so on. None reaches into a sibling's verb. This keeps each step in the staged
  write path independent and auditable, rather than a command quietly chaining
  several mutations.
